concepts.title: Anatomy and physiology of pregnancy
key_points: Blood volume increases substantially in pregnancy, so a large loss can occur before vital signs change
The heart rate is normally somewhat higher and the blood pressure somewhat lower than before pregnancy
Blood is diverted away from the uterus before the mother shows any sign of shock, so the baby suffers first
From roughly mid-pregnancy, lying flat lets the uterus compress the vein returning blood to the heart and drops the pressure
The fix is a left tilt or manual displacement of the uterus to the left, and it takes seconds
The diaphragm is pushed up by the growing uterus, reducing lung capacity and making the patient breathless sooner
The stomach empties more slowly and the sphincter relaxes, so vomiting and aspiration risk are higher
The uterus grows out of the pelvis and becomes the largest, least protected structure in the abdomen
Treating the mother is the only fetal treatment available to you
misconceptions: Reading normal maternal vital signs as reassurance about the pregnancy
Leaving a pregnant patient flat after mid-pregnancy
Forgetting the raised aspiration risk
Treating the fetus rather than the mother

read.plain:
Pregnancy changes almost every system, and several of those changes work against you in an emergency.

Blood volume increases substantially. That is protective for delivery, and it means a pregnant patient can lose a large amount of blood before her pulse and pressure change in any way you would notice.

Her baseline is different too: heart rate normally a little higher, blood pressure normally a little lower. So the numbers you are comparing against are not the ones you would use for a non-pregnant patient of the same age.

Then the consequence that matters most. When volume falls, the body protects the mother's core circulation first, and the uterus is not in that protected category. Blood is diverted away from the placenta before the mother shows any sign of shock at all. By the time maternal vital signs change, the baby has been under-perfused for some time.

Which is why a normal maternal blood pressure is not reassurance about the pregnancy. It is reassurance about the mother, briefly, and nothing more.

Positioning. From roughly the middle of pregnancy onward, the uterus is heavy enough that lying flat on the back compresses the large vein carrying blood from the lower body back to the heart. Less returns, so less is pumped out, and the blood pressure falls — entirely from position, with no blood lost at all.

The fix takes seconds: tilt her to the left, or have somebody push the uterus manually to the left. If she needs spinal precautions, tilt the whole board or scoop rather than turning her on it.

Breathing changes too. The growing uterus pushes the diaphragm upward, so lung capacity falls and she becomes breathless sooner and tires faster. She is also breathing somewhat more deeply at baseline.

The gut slows: the stomach empties more slowly and the sphincter at its top relaxes. Both mean a higher risk of vomiting and of aspirating, which matters for every unconscious or sedated pregnant patient and for anybody you are ventilating.

And anatomically the uterus rises out of the pelvis as pregnancy progresses. It stops being a protected pelvic organ and becomes the largest and least protected structure in the abdomen — which changes what abdominal trauma means entirely.

Running through all of it: treating the mother is the only fetal treatment available to you.
read.standard: Pregnancy produces substantial physiological adaptation. Circulating volume increases considerably, permitting significant haemorrhage prior to alteration in maternal vital signs. Baseline heart rate is modestly elevated and blood pressure modestly reduced relative to the non-pregnant state, altering reference values. Compensatory mechanisms preferentially preserve maternal central circulation, diverting uteroplacental flow prior to maternal decompensation; normal maternal parameters therefore provide no assurance regarding fetal perfusion. From approximately mid-gestation, supine positioning permits gravid uterine compression of the inferior vena cava, reducing venous return and cardiac output with resultant hypotension independent of volume loss; management comprises left lateral tilt or manual leftward uterine displacement, with whole-device tilting where spinal precautions are required. Diaphragmatic elevation reduces functional residual capacity, producing earlier dyspnoea and reduced respiratory reserve, with increased baseline tidal volume. Delayed gastric emptying with reduced lower oesophageal sphincter tone increases regurgitation and aspiration risk, relevant to unconscious patients and during assisted ventilation. Progressive uterine ascent from the pelvis renders it the largest and least protected intra-abdominal structure. Maternal resuscitation constitutes the only available fetal intervention.

eli_new.analogy: Everything about her numbers has shifted, and the baby is the first thing her body stops protecting. The mother looks fine for longer than the pregnancy does.
eli_new.body: Tilt her left. It costs seconds, it needs no equipment, and a pregnant patient left flat can develop a low blood pressure that has nothing to do with her injuries and everything to do with how she was left lying.

concepts.title: Complications of pregnancy
key_points: Pre-eclampsia is a condition of pregnancy with high blood pressure and organ involvement, typically in the second half
Its warning signs are headache, visual disturbance, upper abdominal pain, swelling and a rising blood pressure
Eclampsia is pre-eclampsia that has progressed to seizures, and it is a life-threatening emergency for both
For an eclamptic seizure: protect the airway, give oxygen, keep her on her left side, keep the environment quiet and dim, and transport urgently
Stimulation can provoke further seizures, so minimise light, noise and handling
Placenta previa is a placenta lying over the cervix: painless bright red bleeding, typically later in pregnancy
Placental abruption is the placenta separating from the uterine wall: usually painful, with a tense abdomen, and the bleeding may be concealed
Never perform a vaginal examination in a pregnant patient with bleeding — it can provoke catastrophic haemorrhage
Any bleeding in pregnancy is significant, and concealed bleeding means visible loss tells you nothing
misconceptions: Performing a vaginal examination on a bleeding pregnant patient
Estimating blood loss from what is visible in abruption
Stimulating an eclamptic patient with bright light and noise
Dismissing headache and visual disturbance in late pregnancy

read.plain:
Several complications matter enough that you need to recognise them, and two of them behave in opposite ways.

Pre-eclampsia is a condition specific to pregnancy, usually in the second half, involving raised blood pressure together with organ involvement. What you see are the warning signs: headache, often severe and not relieved by the usual things. Visual disturbance — blurring, flashing lights, spots. Pain in the upper abdomen, classically under the right ribs. Swelling, particularly of the face and hands. And a blood pressure that is rising, which in a pregnant woman whose baseline is normally low is a meaningful change.

Those symptoms in a woman in the second half of pregnancy are not a headache. They are a warning, and they are worth taking to hospital.

Eclampsia is what pre-eclampsia becomes when it progresses to seizures. It is immediately life-threatening for the mother and the baby.

Managing an eclamptic seizure: protect the airway, give oxygen, position her on her left side, and get moving. And do one thing that feels counterintuitive — make the environment quiet and dim. Light, noise and handling can provoke further seizures, so turn things down, speak quietly, and handle her as little as you can. A calm dark ambulance is treatment here.

Then the two bleeding problems, which are easiest to hold as a contrasting pair.

Placenta previa is a placenta sitting over the cervix. As the cervix begins to change late in pregnancy, it bleeds — and the bleeding is typically bright red and, importantly, painless. She is not in pain and she is bleeding.

Placental abruption is the placenta separating from the wall of the uterus. This one usually hurts: abdominal pain, often constant, with a tense or rigid uterus. And the crucial difference — the bleeding may be concealed behind the placenta, so there may be little or nothing visible while she bleeds substantially.

So: previa is painless bleeding you can see; abruption is painful bleeding you may not.

And one absolute rule that covers both: never perform a vaginal examination on a pregnant patient who is bleeding. In placenta previa it can provoke catastrophic haemorrhage. There is no information you could obtain that would justify it, it is outside your scope, and it is one of the few genuinely irreversible mistakes available in this situation.

Treat any bleeding in pregnancy as significant, and remember that in abruption what you can see tells you nothing about what has been lost.
read.standard: Pre-eclampsia is a pregnancy-specific disorder characterised by hypertension with organ involvement, typically manifesting in the second half of gestation. Warning features comprise headache, visual disturbance, right upper quadrant or epigastric pain, oedema particularly of the face and hands, and rising blood pressure, significant against the normally reduced baseline of pregnancy. Eclampsia denotes progression to seizure activity and constitutes an immediate threat to mother and fetus. Management comprises airway protection, oxygen administration, left lateral positioning, minimisation of environmental stimulation as light, noise and handling may precipitate further seizures, and expedited transport. Placenta praevia denotes placental implantation over the cervical os, producing characteristically painless bright red haemorrhage, typically in later pregnancy. Placental abruption denotes premature separation of the placenta from the uterine wall, typically producing abdominal pain with uterine tenderness or rigidity; haemorrhage may be concealed retroplacentally, so visible loss does not reflect actual loss. Vaginal examination is absolutely contraindicated in the bleeding pregnant patient, as it may precipitate catastrophic haemorrhage in praevia; it lies outside scope and yields no information justifying the risk. All bleeding in pregnancy is regarded as significant.

eli_new.analogy: Previa is painless bleeding you can see. Abruption is painful bleeding you may not. That pair is most of what you need.
eli_new.body: A dark, quiet ambulance is treatment in eclampsia. It feels like doing nothing, and light, noise and handling genuinely provoke further seizures — so turning the lights down is an intervention.

concepts.title: Stages of labour and signs of imminent delivery
key_points: Labour has three stages: the first is contractions dilating the cervix, the second is delivery of the baby, the third is delivery of the placenta
The first stage is the longest by far, and usually the one you are transporting during
The decision you actually make is whether to transport or to deliver where you are
Signs of imminent delivery: crowning, contractions close together and strong, an urge to push or to bear down, and a feeling of needing to open the bowels
Crowning — the baby's head visible at the opening — means you are delivering here, not transporting
Ask how many previous deliveries she has had: second and later babies usually come faster
Ask what the contractions are doing — how long they last and how far apart — rather than only how painful they are
An urge to push is a physiological sign, not a preference, and it means the second stage
If you decide to deliver, prepare early: it is much easier to stand down than to catch up
misconceptions: Attempting to transport a crowning patient
Assuming a first-time mother's timeline applies to a fourth baby
Asking only about pain rather than contraction timing
Preparing too late

read.plain:
Labour comes in three stages.

The first stage is contractions doing the work of opening the cervix. It is by far the longest, often many hours, and it is the stage you are usually transporting during.

The second stage is the delivery of the baby itself — from full dilation to the baby being born.

The third stage is the delivery of the placenta, usually within a reasonably short period after the baby.

But the stages are background. The decision you actually make on scene is one question: do I transport this patient, or do I deliver here?

The signs that say deliver here:

Crowning. The baby's head is visible at the vaginal opening. This is not a warning that delivery is approaching — it is delivery happening. If you see crowning, you are delivering where you are.

Contractions close together and strong. Two to three minutes apart, lasting a substantial part of each cycle.

An urge to push or bear down. This is physiological rather than a preference — it happens in the second stage whether she wants it to or not. A woman saying she needs to push is telling you where she is in labour.

A feeling of needing to open her bowels. Same mechanism: pressure from the baby's head. Women frequently report this, and it is a reliable sign that is easily dismissed as embarrassment.

Two questions to ask.

How many babies has she had before? Second and subsequent deliveries are usually considerably faster than a first. A woman on her fourth who says it is coming is almost certainly right, and the timeline you have from a first-time mother does not apply.

What are the contractions doing? Not how painful — how long each one lasts, and how far apart they are. Pain is subjective and varies enormously. Timing is objective and tells you where she is.

And a practical point that matters more than it sounds: if you decide to deliver, prepare early. Get the kit open, get things warm, get somebody positioned. It takes two minutes and it is far easier to stand down a prepared crew than to catch up with a delivery you were not ready for.
read.standard: Labour comprises three stages: the first, cervical dilatation driven by uterine contraction, constituting the longest interval and typically encompassing transport; the second, delivery of the fetus from full dilatation; and the third, delivery of the placenta, usually within a short interval following birth. The operational determination is transport versus on-scene delivery. Indicators of imminent delivery comprise crowning, which represents delivery in progress rather than an approaching event; contractions of short interval and prolonged duration; an urge to bear down, a physiological second-stage phenomenon independent of patient preference; and a sensation of imminent defecation resulting from fetal head pressure, a reliable indicator frequently under-reported. History should establish parity, as second and subsequent deliveries typically progress more rapidly, and contraction frequency and duration in preference to subjective pain assessment. Where delivery on scene is anticipated, preparation should commence early, as standing down a prepared crew is preferable to commencing preparation during delivery.

eli_new.analogy: Crowning is not a warning that delivery is coming. It is delivery, happening, while you are deciding.
eli_new.body: Ask how many babies she has had. A woman on her fourth telling you it is coming now is working from considerably better data than you are, and first-baby timelines do not apply to her at all.

concepts.title: Normal delivery
key_points: Your role is to guide and support the delivery, not to pull — the mother delivers the baby
Support the head as it emerges and allow it to deliver slowly, controlling the speed rather than the direction
Check for a cord around the neck as soon as the head is out: if it is loose, slip it over the head
If the cord is tight around the neck and cannot be freed, it must be clamped in two places and cut between them
After the head delivers it usually turns to one side on its own — let it
Guide the upper shoulder down and then the lower shoulder up; the rest of the body follows quickly and slipperily
Newborns are extremely slippery — have a firm grip and a towel ready
Dry the baby vigorously, keep it warm, and note the time of birth
Do not pull on the cord to deliver the placenta; it delivers itself, and you transport whether or not it has
misconceptions: Pulling on the head or the shoulders
Pulling on the cord to deliver the placenta
Letting the head deliver explosively fast
Failing to have a towel and a firm grip ready
exam_favorites: Checking for a cord around the neck

read.plain:
The first thing to understand is that the mother delivers the baby. You guide, you support, you control the speed, and you catch. You do not pull.

As the head emerges, support it with a flat hand and let it come slowly. The reason for slowing it is that a controlled delivery of the head reduces tearing and gives the baby a gentler transition; the reason for not pushing sideways is that you are not steering, only restraining.

As soon as the head is out, run a finger around the baby's neck to feel for the cord. A cord around the neck is common and usually loose. If it is loose, slip it gently over the head and carry on.

If it is tight around the neck and you cannot free it, it has to be clamped in two places and cut between them, and then the delivery continues immediately. That is a genuine emergency step within your scope where your protocol allows it — know beforehand whether it does, and where your clamps are.

After the head delivers, it usually rotates to one side by itself. That is normal; let it happen rather than holding it straight.

Then the shoulders, and there is a sequence. Guide the head gently downwards to deliver the upper shoulder, then gently upwards to deliver the lower one. Gently is the operative word both times — this is guidance, not traction.

Once the shoulders are out, the rest of the body follows very quickly and very slipperily. Newborns are genuinely difficult to hold. Have a firm grip, support the head and body, and have a towel ready — crews drop babies, and it is entirely preventable by expecting it.

Then: dry the baby vigorously, which also stimulates breathing. Keep it warm — newborns lose heat frighteningly fast, especially wet. Cover the head, which is a large proportion of their surface area. Note the time of birth.

The placenta delivers itself, usually within a reasonably short period. Do not pull on the cord to hurry it. Pulling can tear the cord or, far worse, invert the uterus, which is a catastrophic emergency.

And you do not wait for the placenta. If it has not delivered, transport with the baby and the mother together; if it has, take it with you so it can be examined.
read.standard: The provider guides and supports delivery rather than applying traction; expulsion is maternal. The emerging head is supported with a flat hand, controlling speed of delivery to reduce perineal trauma and permit gradual transition; lateral force is not applied. Following head delivery, the neck is palpated for a nuchal cord, a common finding usually loose and amenable to reduction over the head. A tight nuchal cord that cannot be reduced requires double clamping and division between clamps, with immediate continuation of delivery; providers must establish whether protocol permits this and the location of equipment in advance. External rotation of the head occurs spontaneously and is permitted. Shoulder delivery proceeds by gentle downward guidance to deliver the anterior shoulder followed by gentle upward guidance for the posterior shoulder, with guidance rather than traction throughout. Body delivery follows rapidly with substantial slipperiness; secure grip with head and body support and prepared towel are required. The neonate is dried vigorously, which additionally provides tactile stimulation, kept warm with head covering owing to proportionally large surface area, and the time of birth recorded. Placental delivery occurs spontaneously; cord traction is contraindicated owing to risk of cord avulsion and uterine inversion. Transport does not await placental delivery.

eli_new.analogy: You are not delivering the baby. You are controlling how fast it arrives and making sure you do not drop it.
eli_new.body: Newborns are far slipperier than anybody expects. Have a towel in your hands and expect it, because the alternative is a dropped baby on a bathroom floor and it is completely preventable.

The body came out in about a second and a half, and the newer of the two nearly lost hold of him entirely.

concepts.title: Abnormal deliveries
key_points: A prolapsed cord is the cord presenting before the baby, and it is the one true obstetric emergency you can act on
The cord gets compressed by the baby's head, cutting off its oxygen supply, so the treatment is relieving that pressure
Put the mother head-down with hips elevated, insert a gloved hand and lift the presenting part off the cord, and do not let go
Do not push the cord back in, and keep it warm and moist
A breech delivery presents buttocks or feet first; support what delivers and never pull
In breech, if the head does not deliver, form a V with two fingers to create an airway space beside the baby's face and transport immediately
A nuchal cord around the neck is common: slip it over if loose, clamp and cut if tight and unfreeable
Shoulder dystocia is the head delivering and the shoulders failing to follow; position changes are attempted per protocol and it is a time-critical emergency
Every abnormal delivery is a rapid transport with a pre-alert, because what they need is not available in an ambulance
misconceptions: Pushing a prolapsed cord back inside
Letting go of the presenting part once pressure is relieved
Pulling on a breech baby
Delaying transport in any abnormal delivery

read.plain:
Four situations where delivery does not go normally. In every one of them, the answer includes rapid transport with a pre-alert — because what these patients need is an operating theatre.

A prolapsed cord is the cord coming down ahead of the baby. It is the one obstetric emergency where what you do with your hands genuinely changes the outcome, so it is worth knowing properly.

The problem is compression. The baby's head presses the cord against the pelvis, and the cord is the baby's entire oxygen supply. Relieving that compression is the treatment.

So: put the mother head-down with her hips elevated, using gravity to move the baby off the cord. Then insert a gloved hand and physically lift the presenting part off the cord, and keep it there. You do not let go — not to do anything else, not to help move her, not until somebody at the hospital takes over. That hand stays in place through the entire transport, and it is the treatment.

Do not push the cord back inside. Keep it warm and moist with a saline-moistened dressing, and give the mother high-flow oxygen.

A breech delivery presents buttocks or feet first. Support what delivers as it delivers, and never pull — pulling on a breech baby can trap the head and cause serious injury. Let it come.

If the body delivers and the head does not follow, there is one thing to do: put two fingers into the vagina alongside the baby's face, forming a V to push the vaginal wall away from the nose and mouth and create a space to breathe. Hold that, and transport immediately. The baby can be oxygenated through that gap while you drive.

A nuchal cord — around the neck — is common and usually loose: slip it over the head. If it is tight and cannot be freed, clamp twice and cut between, then deliver immediately.

Shoulder dystocia is the head delivering and the shoulders not following, with the head often pulling back against the perineum. It is genuinely time-critical, because the cord is compressed and the baby cannot breathe. Position changes are attempted per protocol — typically bringing the mother's knees sharply up toward her chest, and repositioning her. Do not pull on the head.

Through all four: rapid transport, a pre-alert that says what you have, and hands doing whatever keeps the baby oxygenated while you travel.
read.standard: Abnormal presentations require expedited transport with prearrival notification, as definitive management requires operative capability. Umbilical cord prolapse denotes cord presentation preceding the fetus, producing cord compression against the pelvis by the presenting part with consequent cessation of fetal oxygenation; it represents the obstetric emergency most amenable to prehospital intervention. Management comprises Trendelenburg or knee-chest positioning to reduce compression, insertion of a gloved hand to elevate the presenting part from the cord, and maintenance of that elevation continuously until relieved by receiving staff. Cord reduction is contraindicated; the cord is kept warm and moist with saline-moistened dressing, and maternal high-concentration oxygen administered. Breech presentation delivers buttocks or lower limbs first; delivered parts are supported without traction, as traction risks head entrapment and injury. Where the body delivers without the head, two fingers are inserted alongside the fetal face forming a V to displace vaginal tissue from the nose and mouth, creating an airway, maintained during immediate transport. Nuchal cord is managed by reduction over the head where loose, or double clamping and division where tight and irreducible. Shoulder dystocia denotes failure of shoulder delivery following head delivery with head retraction; it is time-critical owing to cord compression, managed by positional manoeuvres per protocol including sharp knee-to-chest flexion, without traction on the head.

eli_new.analogy: In a prolapsed cord your hand is the treatment. It goes in, it lifts, and it does not come out again until somebody at the hospital takes over.
eli_new.body: The prolapsed cord one is worth rehearsing in your head, because it is the obstetric emergency where your hands make the difference. Head down, hips up, gloved hand in, lift the head off the cord, and do not let go for anything.

story.title: She did not let go
story.body:
She put her hand in on a bathroom floor and lifted the head off the cord, and then stayed exactly where she was.

Through the carry down the stairs, through the loading, through twenty-two minutes of driving, and into the resuscitation room.

The midwife took over with her hand already in place. That hand had been the baby's entire oxygen supply for half an hour.

concepts.title: Postpartum haemorrhage
key_points: Postpartum haemorrhage is excessive bleeding after delivery and is a leading cause of maternal death
The commonest cause by far is a uterus that has not contracted down after delivering
A contracted uterus feels firm; a uterus that has not contracted feels soft and boggy
Uterine massage is the first-line treatment and it works: firm circular massage of the fundus through the abdomen
Encourage the baby to feed at the breast if the mother is willing, because it stimulates the uterus to contract
Blood loss after delivery is routinely underestimated, and the increased blood volume of pregnancy masks it until late
Never pack the vagina; external pads only, counted
Treat it as shock: position, keep warm, oxygen as indicated, nothing by mouth, rapid transport with a pre-alert
A retained placenta is transported with the patient rather than waited for
misconceptions: Not massaging the uterus because it feels invasive
Underestimating the loss because the mother still looks well
Packing the vagina
Waiting on scene for the placenta while she bleeds

read.plain:
Postpartum haemorrhage is excessive bleeding after delivery, and it remains one of the leading causes of maternal death worldwide. It can be sudden and it can be very large.

The commonest cause, by a considerable margin, is a uterus that has not contracted down after delivering. Understanding why explains the treatment. During pregnancy the uterus receives an enormous blood supply. After the placenta separates, the site where it was attached is a large raw area full of open vessels. The way those vessels close is mechanical: the uterus contracts down hard and squeezes them shut.

If it does not contract, they stay open.

So the assessment is a hand on the abdomen, feeling the fundus — the top of the uterus, just below or around the navel after delivery. A contracted uterus feels firm, like a grapefruit. A uterus that has not contracted feels soft and boggy, and that is your finding.

And the treatment follows directly: uterine massage. Firm, circular massage of the fundus through the abdominal wall. It is not gentle, and it works — the uterus contracts under your hand and the bleeding slows. This is one of the genuinely effective things an EMT can do with nothing but a hand, and it gets skipped because it feels invasive to do to somebody who has just given birth. Explain it and do it.

If the mother is willing, encourage the baby to feed at the breast. Suckling releases hormones that make the uterus contract, and it is free.

Now the reason this is dangerous. Blood loss after delivery is routinely underestimated — it is spread across bedding and towels and it is mixed with fluid. And the increased blood volume of pregnancy means she compensates for a long time, so she can look well while losing a great deal, and then deteriorate quickly.

So do not read her appearance as reassurance. Count what you can — pads, towels — and read her pulse and skin rather than the volume you can see.

Never pack the vagina. External pads only, counted and taken with you.

And manage her as a shocked patient: position her, keep her warm, oxygen as indicated, nothing by mouth because she may go to theatre, and rapid transport with a pre-alert. If the placenta has not delivered, take it and her together and do not wait on scene for it.
read.standard: Postpartum haemorrhage denotes excessive blood loss following delivery and remains a leading cause of maternal mortality. Uterine atony constitutes the predominant aetiology: following placental separation the implantation site presents an extensive vascular surface, haemostasis depending on mechanical compression by uterine contraction. Assessment comprises abdominal palpation of the fundus, located at or below the umbilicus following delivery; a contracted uterus is firm while an atonic uterus is soft and boggy. Fundal massage constitutes first-line management, applied firmly in a circular motion through the abdominal wall, producing uterine contraction and reduced haemorrhage; it represents an effective intervention requiring no equipment and is frequently omitted owing to perceived invasiveness. Breastfeeding, where the mother is willing, stimulates endogenous oxytocin release promoting uterine contraction. Blood loss is routinely underestimated owing to dispersal across bedding and admixture with amniotic fluid, and the hypervolaemia of pregnancy delays haemodynamic manifestation, producing well-appearing patients who subsequently deteriorate rapidly; assessment relies on pulse and cutaneous findings rather than visible volume. Vaginal packing is contraindicated; external pads are used and counted. Management follows shock principles: positioning, normothermia, oxygen as indicated, nil by mouth and expedited transport with prearrival notification. Retained placenta accompanies the patient rather than delaying transport.

eli_new.analogy: After the placenta comes away, the inside of the uterus is a large raw surface full of open vessels. The only thing that closes them is the uterus squeezing, and your hand is what makes it squeeze.
eli_new.body: Uterine massage gets skipped because it feels like a strange thing to do to somebody who has just given birth. It is one of the most effective things you can do with nothing but a hand, and a soft boggy uterus is the finding that tells you to.

concepts.title: Initial newborn care and APGAR
key_points: Almost every newborn needs only three things: warm, dry and stimulate
Drying is both warming and stimulation, and vigorous drying is frequently all the stimulation required
Newborns lose heat extremely fast, so dry them, remove the wet towel, wrap them and cover the head
The three questions that decide everything: is it term, is it breathing or crying, and does it have good tone
A crying baby with good tone needs drying, warming and its mother, and nothing else
APGAR is scored at one minute and five minutes, and it documents progress rather than directing resuscitation
Never delay resuscitation to calculate an APGAR score — the score records what happened, it does not decide it

The heart rate is the single most useful number in a newborn, and it is assessed at the base of the cord or with a stethoscope
misconceptions: Delaying resuscitation to work out an APGAR score
Leaving a newborn in a wet towel
Suctioning routinely when the baby is vigorous
Forgetting to cover the head

read.plain:
The overwhelming majority of newborns need three things and nothing more: warm, dry and stimulate.

And those three overlap neatly, because drying a baby vigorously with a towel does all three jobs at once — it removes wet, it warms, and the friction is stimulation. For most babies, that vigorous drying is the entire resuscitation.

Heat matters more than people expect. Newborns have a very large surface area for their size, almost no insulating fat, and they arrive wet. They lose heat frighteningly fast, and a cold newborn does worse at everything. So dry them, take the wet towel away and replace it with a dry one, wrap them, and cover the head — which is a large proportion of a newborn's surface area and the easiest thing to forget.

Three questions decide what happens next.

Is it term? Is it breathing or crying? Does it have good tone — flexed limbs, moving, rather than floppy?

If all three are yes: dry, warm, and give the baby to its mother. Skin to skin, covered, with a hat on. That is the whole intervention, and it is better than anything else you could do.

If any of those is no, you move into resuscitation, which has its own concept.

Then APGAR, which is frequently misunderstood. It is a score out of ten, assessed at one minute and again at five, made of five components each scored zero, one or two.

Appearance — colour. Pulse — heart rate. Grimace — response to stimulation. Activity — muscle tone. Respiration — breathing effort.

Here is the part that matters: APGAR documents progress. It does not direct resuscitation. You never wait, and you never stop what you are doing, to work out a score. If a baby is not breathing, you are ventilating it — you are not counting up its Appearance. The score is recorded afterwards, from what you observed, and its real value is in the comparison between the one minute and five minute numbers, which shows whether things are improving.

And one number outranks all of it. The heart rate is the single most useful thing you can assess in a newborn, because it tells you whether the resuscitation is working better than anything else does. Feel at the base of the umbilical cord or listen with a stethoscope.
read.standard: The majority of newborns require only warming, drying and stimulation. Vigorous drying provides thermal management, moisture removal and tactile stimulation simultaneously and constitutes sufficient intervention in most cases. Neonatal thermal vulnerability arises from high surface area to mass ratio, minimal subcutaneous insulation and wet presentation; management comprises drying, removal of wet linen, wrapping in dry material and covering the head, which represents a substantial proportion of surface area. Three assessment questions determine subsequent management: gestational maturity, presence of breathing or crying, and muscle tone. Affirmative responses to all three indicate routine care with maternal skin-to-skin contact under covering. Negative response to any indicates progression to resuscitation. APGAR scoring is performed at one and five minutes, comprising Appearance, Pulse, Grimace, Activity and Respiration, each scored zero to two for a maximum of ten. APGAR documents clinical progress and does not direct resuscitation; scoring must never delay or interrupt intervention, and the comparison between one and five minute scores provides the principal value. Heart rate constitutes the single most informative neonatal parameter, indicating resuscitation efficacy, and is assessed at the umbilical base or by auscultation.

eli_new.body: APGAR never decides anything. If a baby is not breathing you are ventilating it, not calculating its Appearance score. The number gets written down afterwards, and its value is in comparing one minute with five.

concepts.title: Neonatal resuscitation
key_points: Newborn resuscitation is almost always a breathing problem, not a heart problem — which reverses the adult priority
Ventilation is the intervention that fixes almost every newborn, and it is the one most often done too late
The sequence: warm, dry and stimulate; then position the airway and clear it only if needed; then assess breathing and heart rate
If the baby is not breathing or the heart rate is below 100, begin positive pressure ventilation
Effective ventilation is judged by the chest rising and by the heart rate improving — the heart rate is the best indicator
If the heart rate stays below 60 despite 30 seconds of effective ventilation, begin compressions
Newborn compressions run at a ratio of 3 compressions to 1 ventilation, with the thumbs encircling the chest
Reassess the heart rate frequently, because it is the measure of whether what you are doing is working
Keep the baby warm throughout — a cold newborn resuscitates badly
misconceptions: Reaching for compressions before ventilation is effective
Suctioning routinely rather than only when needed
Judging ventilation by the bag rather than by chest rise and heart rate
Letting the baby get cold during resuscitation

read.plain:
The single most important idea in newborn resuscitation is that it is a breathing problem, not a heart problem.

An adult in cardiac arrest usually has a heart that has failed with reasonably oxygenated blood still circulating, which is why compressions lead. A newborn is the opposite: its heart is almost always structurally fine, and it is failing because it has not started breathing. Fix the breathing and the heart rate comes back.

Which means ventilation is the intervention, and it is the one most often started too late.

The sequence.

Warm, dry and stimulate. For most babies this is all of it. Position the airway — neutral, not extended, because a newborn's prominent occiput flexes the neck and a slight pad under the shoulders helps. Clear the airway only if there is something obstructing it; routine suctioning of a vigorous baby is not needed and wastes time.

Then assess two things: is it breathing, and what is the heart rate?

If it is not breathing, or gasping, or the heart rate is below 100, start positive pressure ventilation. That is a lower threshold than people expect, and it is deliberate.

Now, how do you know your ventilation is working? Two things. The chest rising — visible, gentle rise, not a heaving one. And the heart rate improving, which is the better indicator of the two. A heart rate that starts climbing is telling you the ventilation is effective in a way nothing else does.

If ventilation is not producing chest rise, fix that before anything else: reposition the head, check the seal, check for obstruction. Ineffective ventilation delivered enthusiastically for two minutes achieves nothing.

If the heart rate remains below 60 despite 30 seconds of effective ventilation — and effective is the operative word — begin compressions.

Newborn compressions use a different ratio from any other patient: three compressions to one ventilation. The technique is thumbs side by side on the lower third of the sternum with your hands encircling the chest. And the ratio exists because it preserves ventilation frequency, which is what this baby actually needs.

Throughout, reassess the heart rate. It is your measure of whether any of this is working.

And keep the baby warm the entire time. A cold newborn resuscitates badly, and it is astonishingly easy to leave one uncovered while concentrating on the airway.
read.standard: Neonatal resuscitation addresses respiratory rather than primary cardiac failure, inverting the adult priority sequence: the neonatal myocardium is typically structurally normal, with bradycardia arising from failure to establish respiration, and resolving with effective ventilation. Ventilation therefore constitutes the principal intervention and is the most frequently delayed. The sequence comprises warming, drying and stimulation; airway positioning in neutral alignment with shoulder padding to offset occipital prominence; airway clearance only where obstruction is present, routine suction of vigorous infants being unnecessary; then assessment of respiration and heart rate. Positive pressure ventilation is indicated for apnoea, gasping, or heart rate below 100 beats per minute. Ventilation efficacy is assessed by visible gentle chest rise and by improvement in heart rate, the latter constituting the superior indicator. Absent chest rise requires correction of position, seal and obstruction before escalation. Chest compressions are indicated where heart rate remains below 60 despite 30 seconds of effective ventilation. Neonatal compression to ventilation ratio is 3:1, performed with the two-thumb encircling technique on the lower sternum, the ratio preserving ventilation frequency. Heart rate is reassessed frequently as the measure of intervention efficacy. Normothermia is maintained throughout, as hypothermia impairs resuscitation.

eli_new.analogy: An adult arrest is a pump that stopped with fuel still in the tank. A newborn is a full tank that never got started, and the starter is the breathing.
eli_new.body: Everything in newborn resuscitation is ventilation until proven otherwise. The heart rate is your read-out of whether it is working — a rising heart rate means your ventilation is effective, and it is a better indicator than anything you can see.

concepts.title: The premature infant
key_points: A premature infant is born before term, and everything that makes newborns vulnerable is exaggerated
Heat loss is the biggest immediate problem: less fat, thinner skin, larger surface area for size
Their lungs may be immature, so they are far more likely to need help breathing
They are small and fragile and need gentle handling, and even ordinary handling is stimulation
They are more prone to infection, so clean technique matters more than usual
Use appropriately sized equipment — an adult or child mask will not seal and will not ventilate
Resuscitate with the same sequence as any newborn: warm, dry, stimulate, ventilate, compress
Do not assume a very premature baby is not viable; begin resuscitation and let the hospital make that decision
Transport to a facility with neonatal capability, and pre-alert so the team is assembled
misconceptions: Deciding on scene that a premature baby is not viable
Using equipment that does not fit
Underestimating how fast a premature baby cools
Handling roughly because of urgency
exam_favorites: Do not judge viability on scene

read.plain:
A premature infant is born before term, and the practical summary is that everything that makes any newborn vulnerable is exaggerated.

Heat loss is the most immediate problem and the one that does the most harm quietly. They have less fat, thinner skin, and an even larger surface area relative to their size. A premature baby cools remarkably fast, and cold makes everything else worse — breathing, circulation, clotting, resuscitation. Dry them, wrap them, cover the head, warm the ambulance beyond what feels comfortable for you, and keep them covered while you work. Whatever your service provides for neonatal warming, use it.

Their lungs may be immature, which means they are considerably more likely to need help breathing than a term baby. Expect to ventilate and be ready before you need to be.

They are small and fragile. Handle them gently — and be aware that with a very small baby, ordinary handling is significant stimulation in itself, so you need less than you think.

They are more prone to infection, so clean technique matters more than usual. Clean hands, clean towels, clean equipment.

Equipment sizing is a practical point that trips crews up. A mask sized for a child or an adult will not seal on a premature face, and a mask that does not seal does not ventilate at all. Know what neonatal equipment your vehicle carries and where it is, before you need it at three in the morning in somebody's bathroom.

The resuscitation sequence itself does not change: warm, dry, stimulate, position the airway, ventilate if not breathing or the heart rate is below 100, compress if below 60 despite effective ventilation.

Now the point that matters most ethically and practically. Do not decide on scene that a very premature baby is not viable. That judgement requires information you do not have — accurate gestation, weight, the response to resuscitation over time — and it is made by people with that information. Begin resuscitation, continue it, transport, and let the hospital make the decision. Withholding on an assumption about gestational age is a decision you cannot undo and cannot reliably make.

And transport to a place with neonatal capability, with a pre-alert so a team is waiting.
read.standard: Preterm infants are born before completion of term gestation, with amplification of all neonatal vulnerabilities. Thermal instability constitutes the principal immediate hazard, arising from reduced subcutaneous adipose tissue, thinner integument and further increased surface area to mass ratio; hypothermia adversely affects respiration, circulation, coagulation and resuscitation efficacy. Management comprises drying, wrapping, head covering, elevated ambient temperature and use of available neonatal warming equipment. Pulmonary immaturity increases the likelihood of requiring ventilatory support, and preparation should precede need. Fragility requires gentle handling, with ordinary handling constituting significant stimulation in very small infants. Increased infection susceptibility warrants clean technique. Equipment sizing is critical: masks sized for larger patients will not achieve a seal and therefore will not ventilate; providers should establish neonatal equipment carriage and location in advance. The resuscitation sequence is unchanged from term infants. Determination of non-viability is not made prehospitally, requiring accurate gestational assessment, weight and response to resuscitation over time; resuscitation is commenced and continued with transport, and viability determination deferred to the receiving facility. Transport is directed to a facility with neonatal capability with prearrival notification.

eli_new.analogy: Everything true of a newborn is more true of a premature one. Thinner, smaller, colder faster, and less able to start breathing on its own.
eli_new.body: Do not make a viability judgement on a bathroom floor. You do not have the gestation, the weight, or any of the information that decision needs. Start, continue, transport, and let people with that information decide.

concepts.title: Approaching the child
key_points: How you approach a child determines how much assessment you actually get
Get down to their eye level — standing over a small child is intimidating and produces resistance
Keep the child with the caregiver wherever possible; separating them makes everything harder
The caregiver is your ally and your information source, and a calm caregiver produces a calm child
Assess toe to head in small children, saving the frightening parts of the exam for last
Infants respond to warmth, gentleness and their caregiver's voice, not to explanation
Toddlers and preschoolers fear separation and strangers, and take things extremely literally
School age children want to be told what is happening and want to be treated honestly
Adolescents want privacy, dignity and to be spoken to directly rather than about
Never lie to a child about whether something will hurt — you lose them for the whole call
misconceptions: Standing over a child and talking down at them
Separating a child from the caregiver unnecessarily
Telling a child something will not hurt when it will
Talking about an adolescent rather than to them
exam_favorites: Toe to head in small children

read.plain:
How you approach a child decides how much assessment you actually get. That is not a soft skill point; it is the difference between a useful examination and a screaming, rigid, uncooperative patient you learn nothing from.

Start with your own position. Get down to their eye level. An adult in a uniform standing over a small child is an intimidating shape, and the response is predictable — withdrawal, crying, resistance. Kneel, sit, get low.

Keep the child with the caregiver wherever it is possible. A child in a parent's arms will tolerate an examination that the same child on a stretcher alone will fight. And the caregiver is your ally twice over: they are your information source, because they know what normal looks like for this child better than you ever will, and their emotional state transmits straight into the child. A calm caregiver produces a calm child. Which means calming the parent is a clinical intervention, not a courtesy.

The examination sequence itself changes. With small children, work toe to head rather than head to toe, saving the parts they find most threatening — the face, the airway, anything near the eyes — for last. By then they have seen you touch their foot and their knee and their belly without anything bad happening.

Then adjust for developmental stage, because what frightens a child changes completely as they grow.

Infants respond to warmth, gentleness and a familiar voice. They do not respond to explanation, so do not waste time on it — be warm and keep the caregiver close.

Toddlers and preschoolers fear separation and strangers most of all, and they are startlingly literal. Say you are going to take their blood pressure and they may reasonably expect you to take something away and keep it. Use simple, concrete language, let them touch equipment, and offer choices where the answer does not matter — which arm, which finger — because a small amount of control goes a long way.

School age children want to be told what is happening, and they want honesty. They can cooperate remarkably well if you explain first.

Adolescents want privacy and dignity, and they want to be spoken to directly rather than discussed over their heads. Give them the chance to answer questions away from a parent where that is appropriate and safe.

And the rule that spans all of them: never tell a child something will not hurt when it will. You get one chance at that, and when it turns out to be a lie you have lost their trust for the rest of the call and possibly for the next crew as well. Say that it will pinch, say how long, and then be right.
read.standard: The approach to paediatric patients materially determines assessment yield. Positioning at the child's eye level reduces the intimidation of an adult provider in uniform standing over a small patient, which predictably produces withdrawal and resistance. Maintaining caregiver proximity improves tolerance of examination; the caregiver additionally serves as the authority on the child's baseline and transmits emotional state to the child, rendering caregiver reassurance a clinical intervention. Examination sequence in small children proceeds toe to head, deferring threatening components involving the face and airway. Approach is modified by developmental stage: infants respond to warmth, gentleness and familiar voice rather than explanation; toddlers and preschool children experience stranger and separation anxiety and interpret language literally, benefiting from concrete phrasing, equipment familiarisation and inconsequential choices conferring control; school-age children cooperate with prior explanation and require honesty; adolescents require privacy, dignity, direct address and, where appropriate and safe, opportunity to answer independently of caregivers. Providers must not misrepresent whether a procedure will cause pain, as loss of trust compromises the remainder of the encounter and subsequent care.

eli_new.body: Calming the parent is treatment. Their state goes straight into the child, and a frightened parent will hand you a frightened patient every single time.

concepts.title: How children differ anatomically and physiologically
key_points: A child is not a small adult — the differences change what goes wrong and how fast
Bigger head and prominent occiput: the neck flexes when they lie flat, so pad under the shoulders
Bigger tongue relative to the mouth, and a narrower, softer, more collapsible airway
Small amounts of swelling or secretions block a small airway far more than a large one
Ribs are more horizontal and more cartilaginous, so children depend heavily on the diaphragm
Because the ribs are flexible, severe internal injury can occur without any rib fracture
Larger surface area for their size means they lose heat fast, including during resuscitation
Blood volume is smaller in absolute terms, so a loss that looks minor can be a large fraction of it
Children compensate extremely well and then decompensate abruptly — the crash is sudden, not gradual
The liver and spleen are relatively large and less protected by the rib cage
misconceptions: Treating a child as a scaled-down adult
Assuming no rib fracture means no chest injury
Extending the neck to open an infant airway
Underestimating how fast a child cools

read.plain:
A child is not a small adult. That phrase gets repeated until it means nothing, so here is what it actually changes.

The head. Children have proportionally larger heads with a prominent occiput. Lay a small child flat on a board and the head pushes the neck into flexion, which narrows the airway you were trying to protect. The fix is a pad under the shoulders to bring the airway back to neutral — the opposite of the adult, where you might pad the head.

The airway itself. The tongue is proportionally bigger and more likely to obstruct. The airway is narrower, and the tissues are softer and more collapsible, which means hyperextending the neck can kink the airway shut rather than open it. Neutral to slightly extended, no more.

And there is a geometry point worth understanding rather than memorising: a small amount of swelling in a small tube takes away a far larger proportion of the opening than the same swelling in a big tube. This is why croup and epiglottitis and a mouthful of secretions do to a child what they would not do to an adult. Small airways are unforgiving.

The chest. A child's ribs sit more horizontally and are far more cartilaginous — flexible rather than rigid. Two consequences. First, they cannot increase their tidal volume much by moving the ribs, so they depend heavily on the diaphragm, which is why anything pressing on the abdomen or a distended stomach impairs breathing. Second, and much more important: force passes through a flexible chest wall into the organs without breaking the ribs. Severe lung or organ injury with no fracture at all is entirely possible. A rib fracture in a child means enormous force was applied.

Temperature. A larger surface area for their size and less insulation means they cool fast, and cold makes everything worse. Keep them covered, including during resuscitation, when it is easiest to forget.

Blood volume. Children have more blood per kilogram but much less in absolute terms. A volume of blood that would be trivial in an adult can be a substantial fraction of a small child's circulating volume. Do not judge blood loss by the size of the puddle; judge it against the size of the patient.

Organs. The liver and spleen are relatively large and sit lower and less protected by the rib cage, so abdominal trauma injures them readily.

And the single most important physiological point, which deserves its own concept: children compensate extraordinarily well. Their cardiovascular reserve is excellent, and they can maintain a normal-looking blood pressure while in serious trouble. Then the compensation fails, and it fails abruptly rather than gradually. The deterioration is a cliff, not a slope. Which means a child who looks borderline is a child you act on now, not one you watch.
read.standard: Paediatric anatomy and physiology differ from adult in ways that alter both pathology and rate of deterioration. Proportionally larger head and prominent occiput produce cervical flexion in supine positioning, requiring shoulder padding to restore neutral airway alignment, inverse to adult practice. Airway differences comprise proportionally larger tongue, narrower calibre and softer, more collapsible tissues, such that hyperextension may occlude rather than open the airway. Reduced airway calibre means a given degree of oedema or secretion occupies a substantially greater proportion of the lumen, accounting for the disproportionate impact of upper airway pathology. Thoracic ribs are more horizontally oriented and more cartilaginous, limiting tidal volume augmentation by rib movement and producing diaphragmatic dependence, such that abdominal pressure or gastric distension impairs ventilation; flexibility additionally permits transmission of force to underlying organs without fracture, and paediatric rib fracture implies substantial force. Increased surface area to mass ratio with reduced insulation produces rapid heat loss. Circulating volume is greater per unit mass but smaller in absolute terms, so a given haemorrhage represents a larger proportional loss. The liver and spleen are relatively large and less protected by the thoracic cage. Physiologically, paediatric compensatory reserve is substantial, maintaining apparently normal blood pressure during significant compromise, with decompensation occurring abruptly rather than progressively.

eli_new.body: The flexible rib cage is the trap. Force passes straight through it into the lungs and liver without breaking anything, so a child with a normal-looking chest can have a badly injured one underneath.

concepts.title: The pediatric assessment triangle
key_points: The paediatric assessment triangle is a structured way of forming a general impression from across the room
It uses only what you can see and hear — no equipment, no touching the child
Three arms: Appearance, Work of Breathing, and Circulation to the Skin
Appearance asks whether the brain is being adequately perfused and oxygenated
TICLS for appearance: Tone, Interactiveness, Consolability, Look or gaze, Speech or cry
Work of breathing covers abnormal sounds, positioning, retractions, nasal flaring and head bobbing
Circulation to the skin covers pallor, mottling and cyanosis
It answers two questions: how sick, and which system is failing
It takes seconds and it happens before you lay a hand on the child
Abnormal appearance alone is significant — a child who is not behaving like a child is a sick child
misconceptions: Skipping the triangle and going straight to vital signs
Touching the child before forming the impression
Treating a quiet, floppy child as settled
Assuming a normal appearance rules out serious illness

read.plain:
The paediatric assessment triangle is a structured way of doing what experienced people do instinctively: forming a general impression from the doorway, before you touch anything.

And its great virtue is that it needs no equipment at all. Only what you can see and hear. It takes a few seconds, it happens before you lay a hand on the child, and it answers two questions: how sick is this child, and which system is in trouble?

Three arms.

Appearance. This is the most important one, because it is asking whether the brain is being adequately perfused and oxygenated. A brain that is short of either does not behave normally, and in a child that shows up in behaviour long before it shows up in a number. The memory aid is TICLS. Tone — are they moving normally or floppy? Interactiveness — do they engage with you, reach for things, notice what is happening? Consolability — can the caregiver settle them, or is the crying inconsolable? Look or gaze — do they fix on faces, or is there a vacant stare? Speech or cry — is it strong and appropriate, or weak, and is there any cry at all?

And this is where the quiet child trap lives. A screaming child is using energy and interacting, which is reassuring. A quiet, floppy child who does not object to strangers is frequently the sicker one. Do not mistake silence for settled.

Work of breathing. Everything visible and audible about the effort of breathing. Abnormal sounds — stridor, grunting, wheezing. Abnormal positioning — sitting forward, tripoding, refusing to lie down, the sniffing position. Retractions — skin pulling in between or below the ribs or at the neck. Nasal flaring. Head bobbing in infants. All of it says the child is working harder than they should.

Circulation to the skin. Pallor, mottling, cyanosis. What the periphery looks like when the body is prioritising the core.

Now the useful part: the pattern tells you which system is failing. Breathing abnormal but appearance and skin normal points to respiratory distress. Appearance also abnormal points to respiratory failure. Appearance and skin abnormal with normal breathing points towards shock. All three abnormal is a child in serious trouble.

The triangle does not replace anything. You still do your primary assessment, your vital signs, your history. What it gives you is a rapid, structured first impression, and a reason to act quickly on a child who does not look right before any number has told you so.

And hold on to that last point, because it is the whole value. A child who is not behaving like a child is a sick child, even when everything you can measure is normal.
read.standard: The paediatric assessment triangle provides a structured general impression formed without equipment or physical contact, using visual and auditory information alone, and addresses two questions: severity of illness and the physiological system involved. It comprises three components. Appearance reflects adequacy of cerebral perfusion and oxygenation, assessed by the mnemonic TICLS: Tone, Interactiveness, Consolability, Look or gaze, and Speech or cry. Abnormal appearance may precede measurable abnormality; a quiet, hypotonic child who does not resist strangers frequently represents greater severity than a vigorously crying child. Work of breathing encompasses audible abnormal sounds including stridor, grunting and wheeze; abnormal positioning including tripoding, sniffing position and refusal to lie supine; retractions; nasal flaring; and head bobbing in infants. Circulation to the skin encompasses pallor, mottling and cyanosis. Component patterns indicate the system involved: isolated abnormal work of breathing suggests respiratory distress; addition of abnormal appearance suggests respiratory failure; abnormal appearance and circulation with normal breathing suggests shock; abnormality of all three indicates severe compromise. The triangle supplements rather than replaces primary assessment, vital signs and history, and justifies early intervention in a child whose behaviour is abnormal despite normal measured parameters.

eli_new.body: The quiet child is the trap. A screaming child is spending energy and interacting with you. A floppy, silent child who does not mind a stranger touching them is usually the sicker one.

concepts.title: Respiratory distress and respiratory failure
key_points: Respiratory problems are the commonest path to paediatric cardiac arrest, which makes this the highest-value chapter in paediatrics
Distress is a child working hard and succeeding; failure is a child working hard and losing
Distress looks loud and busy: retractions, flaring, grunting, noisy breathing, tripoding, a child who is alert and frightened
Failure looks quiet: decreasing effort, decreasing tone, altered mental status, a slowing heart rate
The quiet chest and the calm child are the most dangerous findings in paediatric respiratory illness
A falling heart rate in a struggling child is a very late and very ominous sign
Let a child in distress hold whatever position they have chosen — they have found the one that works
Agitating a child who is compensating can tip them into failure, so keep them calm and with the caregiver
Treat failure by assisting ventilation, and do not wait for arrest to do it
Recognising failure early is the single most useful paediatric skill there is
misconceptions: Reading a quiet chest as improvement
Reading a calm child as settled rather than exhausted
Forcing a child in distress to lie down
Upsetting a compensating child with unnecessary procedures

read.plain:
Respiratory problems are the commonest route to paediatric cardiac arrest. Children rarely arrest from a heart that fails on its own; they arrest because breathing failed first and the heart followed. Which makes this the highest-value thing in paediatrics: if you recognise and treat respiratory failure early, you prevent the arrest entirely.

The distinction that matters is between distress and failure.

Distress is a child working hard and succeeding. The work is visible and audible, and that is the point — you can see the compensation happening. Retractions between and below the ribs and at the neck. Nasal flaring. Grunting, which is an infant trying to hold pressure in the lungs. Noisy breathing. Tripoding, or the sniffing position, or a flat refusal to lie down. A fast rate. And crucially, the child is alert, frightened, and objecting. The system is stressed and holding.

Failure is a child working hard and losing. And here is the part that catches people, because failure does not look worse in the obvious way. It looks quieter.

The effort decreases, because they are exhausted. The noise decreases, because less air is moving — a chest that has gone quiet after being noisy has not improved, it has stopped ventilating. The muscle tone decreases. Mental status changes: drowsy, floppy, not interacting, not fighting you any more. And the heart rate, which was fast, begins to fall. Bradycardia in a struggling child is very late and very ominous, and it is usually the last thing before arrest.

So the dangerous findings in paediatric respiratory illness are all findings that look like improvement. The quiet chest. The calm child. The slowing heart rate. If any of those appear in a child who was loud and fast ten minutes ago, they are worse, not better.

Two practical points.

Let a child in distress keep whatever position they have chosen. They have found the one that works, and they know more about their own airway than you do. Forcing them flat for your convenience can be actively harmful.

And keep them calm. Agitation increases oxygen demand, and a child who is just barely compensating can be tipped into failure by crying. Which means a procedure that upsets a marginal child needs to be worth the cost. Keep the caregiver close, keep your voice low, and leave them alone where you can.

Treatment of failure is assisted ventilation, and the mistake is waiting. Do not wait for arrest to begin ventilating a child who has stopped compensating.
read.standard: Respiratory pathology constitutes the predominant pathway to paediatric cardiac arrest, arrest typically following respiratory rather than primary cardiac failure; early recognition and treatment of respiratory failure therefore prevents arrest. Respiratory distress denotes effective compensation, characterised by visible and audible work: intercostal, subcostal and suprasternal retractions, nasal flaring, grunting, audible abnormal breath sounds, tripod or sniffing positioning, refusal of supine position, tachypnoea, with preserved alertness and appropriate distress behaviour. Respiratory failure denotes failing compensation and presents paradoxically as reduced rather than increased activity: diminished respiratory effort from fatigue, diminished breath sounds reflecting reduced air movement, decreased muscle tone, altered mental status with reduced interactiveness, and bradycardia. A previously noisy chest that becomes quiet indicates deteriorating ventilation rather than improvement, and bradycardia in a compromised child is a late and preminal finding. Management principles include permitting the child to maintain self-selected positioning, minimising agitation as increased oxygen demand may precipitate failure in a marginally compensating child, maintaining caregiver proximity, and deferring non-essential procedures. Failure is managed by assisted ventilation, initiated before arrest occurs.

eli_new.body: Everything that looks like improvement in a struggling child — the chest going quiet, the child settling, the heart rate coming down — is the list of signs that they are running out. Be suspicious of good news that arrives too easily.

concepts.title: Pediatric shock
key_points: Children compensate for shock exceptionally well, which is exactly what makes it dangerous
They maintain a normal-looking blood pressure until very late by increasing rate and clamping down peripherally
Hypotension in a child is a late and ominous finding, not an early one
The early signs are all peripheral: tachycardia, poor capillary refill, cool mottled skin, weak peripheral pulses
Altered appearance is an early and important sign, because the brain notices poor perfusion first
Decreased urine output — fewer wet nappies — is useful history from the caregiver
Dehydration from vomiting and diarrhoea is a common paediatric cause and is easy to underestimate
Blood loss that looks small can be a large fraction of a small child's circulating volume
Never wait for a blood pressure to fall before treating a child as being in shock
Keep them warm, position appropriately, give oxygen per protocol, and transport without delay
misconceptions: Waiting for hypotension before treating
Reassurance from a normal blood pressure
Underestimating blood loss because the volume looks small
Letting a shocked child get cold

read.plain:
Children compensate for shock exceptionally well, and that is exactly what makes paediatric shock dangerous. Their cardiovascular reserve is excellent. They increase their heart rate, clamp down the periphery hard, and maintain a normal-looking blood pressure while a substantial fraction of their circulating volume is gone.

So the single most important thing to carry away is this: a normal blood pressure in a child tells you almost nothing reassuring. Hypotension in a child is late. By the time the pressure falls, compensation has already failed, and what follows is fast.

Which means you have to read the signs that come earlier, and they are all peripheral or behavioural.

Tachycardia is usually first, though it is non-specific — fever, fear and pain all do it too. Capillary refill lengthens. The skin goes cool, pale, then mottled. Peripheral pulses weaken while central pulses are still strong, which is the body prioritising the core and is a useful comparison to make deliberately — feel both.

And appearance changes, which brings the assessment triangle straight back in. The brain notices poor perfusion early, so a child who is less interactive, less consolable, floppier or vacant is telling you about their perfusion before any number does.

One piece of history worth asking for specifically: urine output. How many wet nappies today, compared with a normal day? Caregivers know this, and a dramatic reduction is real evidence of volume depletion.

On causes: dehydration from vomiting and diarrhoea is extremely common in children and is easy to underestimate, because there is nothing dramatic to look at. And in trauma, remember the volume point from the anatomy concept — a child's total blood volume is small, so a loss that would be unremarkable in an adult can be a large share of theirs. Judge blood loss against the size of the patient, not against the size of the puddle.

Management at EMT level is unglamorous and effective. Oxygen per protocol. Position appropriately. Control any bleeding. Keep them warm, because a cold child does worse and shocked children lose heat quickly. And transport without delay, because the definitive treatment is not in your vehicle.

The discipline to build is treating on the early signs. If you wait for the blood pressure to confirm what the skin and the appearance already told you, you have waited too long.
read.standard: Paediatric compensatory capacity for shock is substantial, maintaining apparently normal blood pressure through tachycardia and peripheral vasoconstriction despite significant volume depletion. Hypotension therefore constitutes a late finding indicating compensatory failure, with rapid subsequent deterioration; normal blood pressure does not exclude significant shock. Early indicators are peripheral and behavioural: tachycardia, though non-specific given fever, anxiety and pain as confounders; prolonged capillary refill; cool, pale, then mottled skin; and diminished peripheral pulses with preserved central pulses, a comparison that should be performed deliberately. Altered appearance reflects early cerebral hypoperfusion and precedes measurable change. Reduced urine output, elicited as reduction in wet nappies against the child's baseline, provides useful corroborating history. Dehydration secondary to vomiting and diarrhoea is a common and readily underestimated paediatric aetiology. In trauma, small absolute circulating volume means apparently modest haemorrhage may represent substantial proportional loss, and loss should be assessed relative to patient size. Prehospital management comprises oxygen per protocol, appropriate positioning, haemorrhage control, maintenance of normothermia, and expeditious transport. Treatment is initiated on early findings rather than deferred pending hypotension.

eli_new.analogy: A child holds their blood pressure up the way someone holds a heavy door — completely, right up until the moment they cannot hold it at all.
eli_new.body: Never let a normal blood pressure reassure you about a child. It is the last thing to go, and when it goes, so do they.

concepts.title: Pediatric seizures and fever
key_points: Seizure care in a child is the same as in an adult: protect them, do not restrain them, and do not put anything in the mouth
Protect the head, clear the space, position for airway protection after the seizure, and give oxygen per protocol
Febrile seizures happen in young children with a rising temperature and are usually brief and self-limiting
A febrile seizure is terrifying for the caregiver and usually benign for the child — both of those facts need managing
Any child who has seized needs transport and evaluation, because the cause is what matters
A seizure lasting a long time, or repeating without recovery in between, is an emergency
Look for other causes: head injury, low blood sugar, poisoning, infection, hypoxia
Ask about fever, recent illness, medications in the house, head injury and any seizure history
Cool the child sensibly rather than aggressively — remove excess clothing, do not use ice or cold water
