misconceptions: Restraining a seizing child
Putting something in the mouth
Aggressive cooling with ice or cold water
Treating a febrile seizure as needing no evaluation

read.plain:
Seizure care in a child is the same as in an adult, and the basics do not change. Protect them from injury. Do not restrain them. Do not put anything in the mouth — that instruction is old and wrong and still occasionally attempted. Protect the head, move furniture away, note the time and what you actually saw, and once the seizure stops, position for airway protection, suction if needed and give oxygen per protocol.

What is distinctively paediatric is the febrile seizure. Young children can seize when their temperature rises — and it is the rise rather than the absolute height that seems to matter. They are typically brief, generalised and self-limiting, and they stop before or shortly after you arrive.

Here is the practical shape of that call. A febrile seizure is usually benign for the child and absolutely terrifying for the caregiver, who has quite often just watched what they believed was their child dying. Both of those facts need managing. Treat the child, and then genuinely treat the parent — explain what happened, explain what you are doing, and do not dismiss it, because the fear is real even when the seizure was not dangerous.

Every child who has seized is transported and evaluated. Not because the seizure itself needs hospital treatment, but because the cause does, and you cannot exclude the important causes on a living-room floor.

So keep a differential running. Head injury. Low blood sugar, which is worth checking and correcting per protocol. Poisoning or ingestion, especially in a toddler who was briefly unsupervised — ask what is in the house. Infection, including meningitis. Hypoxia. Fever is the commonest explanation in a young child, and assuming it is the explanation is how the others get missed.

Ask specifically: was there a fever, has the child been unwell, does the child have a seizure history and is this one different from their usual, what medications are in the house, and could there have been a head injury.

On cooling: sensible, not aggressive. Remove excess clothing and blankets. Do not use ice, cold water or alcohol — they can cause shivering, which raises temperature, and they are unpleasant for a child who has just had a very bad few minutes.

And expect the postictal period. A child who has seized may be drowsy, confused and unresponsive-looking for some time. That is expected. What is not expected is failing to gradually improve, or seizing again without recovering in between, or a seizure that simply does not stop — each of which is an emergency and a reason to move.
read.standard: Paediatric seizure management follows general principles: protection from injury without restraint, avoidance of oral insertion of any object, cranial protection, environmental clearance, documentation of duration and observed features, and post-ictal airway positioning with suction and oxygen per protocol. Febrile seizures occur in young children in association with rising temperature, with rate of rise apparently more relevant than absolute value, and are characteristically brief, generalised and self-limiting. Such events are typically benign for the patient while producing marked caregiver distress, requiring explicit explanation and reassurance alongside clinical care. All children who have seized require transport and evaluation, as determination of aetiology cannot be completed prehospitally. Differential considerations include head injury, hypoglycaemia, which should be assessed and corrected per protocol, toxic ingestion particularly in unsupervised toddlers, infection including meningitis, and hypoxia; attribution to fever without consideration of alternatives risks missing significant causes. History should address fever, recent illness, prior seizure history and deviation from the patient's usual pattern, medications accessible in the environment, and possible head injury. Cooling should be moderate, comprising removal of excess clothing; ice, cold water and alcohol are contraindicated as shivering elevates temperature. Post-ictal drowsiness and confusion are expected; failure to improve progressively, recurrent seizures without interval recovery, and prolonged seizure activity constitute emergencies.

concepts.title: Sudden infant death and the unexpected infant event
key_points: Sudden infant death is the sudden, unexplained death of an infant, typically found during sleep
Begin resuscitation unless there are obvious signs of irreversible death, and follow your protocol
Do not speculate about cause and never suggest or imply blame to the family
Observe and document the scene factually: position found, surroundings, temperature, time last seen well

Implying blame to caregivers
Leaving a well-looking infant at home after an unexplained event

read.plain:
Sudden infant death is the sudden and unexplained death of an infant, typically found during sleep, where nothing in the history or the scene accounts for it. It remains unexplained after investigation, which is the essential point — it is not a thing you can diagnose on scene, and you should not try.

What you do on scene is straightforward to state and very hard to do.

Begin resuscitation unless there are obvious signs of irreversible death, and follow your protocol and medical direction on that question. Most systems ask you to start.

Do not speculate about cause. Not to the family, not to each other in earshot, not in your documentation. And never suggest or imply blame, including by the questions you ask or the way you ask them. Parents in this situation are already searching for what they did wrong, and a badly phrased question will stay with them permanently.

Observe the scene carefully and document it factually. The position the infant was found in. The surroundings — bedding, objects, sleeping surface, who else was in the bed. Room temperature. When the infant was last seen well, and by whom. Any medication or illness. This information genuinely matters to the investigation that follows, and you are the only clinician who will ever see that room as it was.

And hold on to the distinction that governs all of it: document what you observe, not what you conclude. "Infant found prone on an adult bed with two pillows and a duvet" is an observation. "Infant suffocated by bedding" is a conclusion, it is not yours to make, and it can do real damage.

Be honest about the other thing too. These are among the hardest calls in EMS, and they affect experienced people badly. The crew needs support afterwards, and asking for it is not weakness. Know what your service provides before you need it.

Then the related presentation: the brief resolved unexplained event. An infant has an episode — a change in colour, a change in tone, a change in breathing, or a period of altered responsiveness — which frightens the caregiver badly and has completely resolved by the time you arrive. The infant in front of you looks entirely normal.

The rule is that the infant still needs transport and evaluation. A normal-looking infant after such an event has not been cleared of anything; the causes that matter are not visible to you, and they are not excluded by a baby who is currently smiling at the ceiling.

And take the caregiver's account seriously. They watched something that frightened them enough to call, they know this infant, and your reassurance should never take the form of suggesting they imagined it.
read.standard: Sudden infant death denotes the sudden, unexplained death of an infant, typically discovered during sleep, remaining unexplained following investigation; prehospital diagnosis is not possible or appropriate. Resuscitation is initiated unless obvious signs of irreversible death are present, in accordance with protocol and medical direction. Providers must not speculate as to cause in any setting, including documentation and discussion within family hearing, and must avoid any suggestion or implication of caregiver culpability, including through phrasing of history questions. Scene observation and factual documentation are important contributions to subsequent investigation and should record position found, bedding and sleep surface, objects present, co-sleeping arrangements, ambient temperature, time and person last observing the infant well, and relevant illness or medication. Documentation must record observation rather than conclusion. These incidents carry substantial provider psychological impact and warrant crew support following the call. A brief resolved unexplained event describes an episode of altered colour, tone, breathing or responsiveness in an infant that has fully resolved at the time of assessment. Transport and evaluation remain indicated despite apparently normal findings, as relevant aetiologies are not excluded by current normality, and caregiver accounts should be accorded credibility.

eli_new.analogy: You are the only clinician who will ever see that room the way it was. Describe it, and leave the conclusions to people whose job that is.
eli_new.body: The line that protects everyone is observation versus conclusion. Write where the infant was and what was in the cot. Do not write why.

concepts.title: Recognising abuse and neglect
key_points: EMS providers are mandated reporters in most systems — know your obligation before you need it
You report suspicion, not proof, and you are not required to be certain
The strongest single indicator is a history that does not match the injury
Also concerning: a history that changes, a delay in seeking care, or an injury impossible for the child's developmental stage
Injuries in unusual places, patterned injuries, and injuries of clearly different ages raise suspicion
Neglect can present as poor hygiene, malnutrition, untreated conditions or an unsafe environment
Do not confront or accuse the caregiver — it endangers the child and it ends the call
Your job on scene is the child's medical care, safe transport, and factual documentation

read.plain:
In most systems EMS providers are mandated reporters, which means the law requires you to report suspected abuse or neglect. Find out what your specific obligation is and how the reporting is done before you are standing in a house needing to know.

And take the weight off yourself with this: you report suspicion, not proof. You are not the investigator, you are not required to be certain, and you are not deciding what happened. You are reporting that something concerned you, to people whose job is to find out.

What concerns you, in practice?

The strongest single indicator is a history that does not match the injury. A mechanism described that could not produce what you are looking at, or an injury far more severe than the story accounts for. Related to that: a history that changes between tellings or between people, a substantial unexplained delay in seeking care, or an injury that is impossible for the child's developmental stage — an infant who cannot yet roll over does not roll off things.

Then the physical findings. Injuries in unusual places, rather than the shins, knees, elbows and foreheads where mobile children injure themselves. Patterned injuries that suggest the shape of an object. Injuries that are clearly of different ages. Burns with unusual patterns or distributions.

Neglect looks different and is easy to miss because there is no single event: persistently poor hygiene, malnutrition, untreated medical conditions, a child dressed inappropriately for the weather, an unsafe or grossly unsuitable environment.

None of these proves anything by itself. Children do get hurt in odd ways, families do live in difficult circumstances, and a single finding is a reason to look carefully rather than a verdict.

Now the most important practical rule: do not confront or accuse the caregiver. It does not help. It can make the scene unsafe for you, it can make things worse for the child after you leave, and it can end the call — a caregiver who becomes hostile may refuse transport, and then the child stays. Stay professional, stay neutral, and get the child to hospital.

Your job on scene is three things: the child's medical care, safe transport, and factual documentation.

Document objectively. Quote what people said, in quotation marks, attributed to who said it. Describe injuries by location, size, colour and appearance, without interpreting them. "Four-centimetre linear bruise to the left posterior thigh" is documentation. "Bruise from a belt" is an interpretation you cannot support.

Then make the report through your procedure. Do not assume the hospital or another agency will do it. And it is worth knowing that reporting in good faith is legally protected in most jurisdictions — the system is built to make reporting the safe thing to do.
read.standard: EMS providers hold mandated reporter status in most jurisdictions, and providers should establish their specific statutory obligation and reporting mechanism in advance. The threshold for reporting is suspicion rather than proof; providers are not investigators and certainty is not required. The most significant indicator is incongruence between reported mechanism and observed injury, including injury severity disproportionate to the stated history. Additional concerning features include inconsistent histories across tellings or informants, unexplained delay in seeking care, and injury incompatible with the child's developmental capabilities. Physical findings raising concern include injuries at atypical anatomical sites rather than the shins, knees, elbows and forehead typical of accidental paediatric injury; patterned injuries suggesting an implement; injuries of differing apparent ages; and burns of atypical pattern or distribution. Neglect may manifest as persistent poor hygiene, malnutrition, untreated medical conditions, inappropriate clothing for conditions, or unsafe environment. Individual findings are not diagnostic. Providers must not confront or accuse caregivers, as this may compromise scene safety, worsen the child's subsequent circumstances, and precipitate transport refusal. Prehospital responsibilities comprise medical care, safe transport and objective documentation using direct quotation with attribution and injury description by location, dimension, colour and appearance without interpretation. Reporting proceeds through the provider's own procedure and is generally afforded legal protection when made in good faith.

eli_new.analogy: You are not deciding what happened. You are telling the people whose job that is that something did not add up.
eli_new.body: The single most useful question is whether the story explains the injury. When it does not, that is the finding — and it is enough to report on its own.

Nobody said anything about that in the house. They treated the arm and drove.

The report said what the caregiver had said, in quotation marks, and what the infant could and could not do. That was all it needed to say.

concepts.title: Pediatric trauma considerations
key_points: Trauma is a leading cause of death in children, and blunt mechanisms predominate
Because the body is smaller, force is distributed across more of it — multi-system injury is the norm, not the exception
The large head means head injury is common and often the most significant injury present
Flexible bones transmit force to organs without breaking, so serious injury can exist with no fracture
Assume the mechanism and treat for what it could have caused, rather than what you can see
Airway management follows the paediatric rules: neutral position, pad the shoulders, do not over-extend
Keep them warm — trauma, exposure and a large surface area combine to cool a child fast
Blood loss that appears modest may be a large fraction of a small circulating volume
They compensate well then crash, so transport decisions are made early rather than after deterioration
Transport to a facility with paediatric capability where your system provides one
misconceptions: Reassurance from the absence of fractures
Waiting for deterioration before deciding on transport
Over-extending the neck during airway management
Letting an injured child get cold

read.plain:
Trauma is a leading cause of death in children, and the mechanisms are overwhelmingly blunt — falls, being struck by vehicles, motor vehicle collisions, bicycles.

The governing idea is one of geometry. A child is small, so the same amount of force is distributed across a much larger proportion of the body. Multi-system injury is therefore the normal presentation rather than the unusual one. An adult struck by a car may have one badly injured leg; a child struck by the same car has taken that force through the legs, the abdomen, the chest and the head. Look everywhere, always.

The head deserves particular attention because it is proportionally large, relatively heavy and frequently leads in a fall. Head injury is common in paediatric trauma and is very often the most significant injury present. Watch mental status carefully, and take a change in it seriously.

Then bring back the flexibility point from the anatomy concept, because it matters more in trauma than anywhere else. A child's bones and rib cage bend. Force passes through to the organs underneath without necessarily breaking anything. Which means the absence of fractures is not reassurance — a chest that looks intact can conceal badly injured lungs, and an abdomen with no external mark can conceal an injured liver or spleen.

This leads to the central discipline of paediatric trauma: assume the mechanism. Treat for what the forces involved could have caused, not for what you can currently see. Children hide injury well, and then stop hiding it suddenly.

Some specifics.

Airway management follows the paediatric rules. Neutral position, pad under the shoulders to offset the occiput, and do not over-extend a soft, collapsible airway.

Temperature is a genuine problem. Trauma, exposure, cut-away clothing and a large surface area combine to cool a child fast, and hypothermia worsens bleeding and outcomes. Cover them, warm the compartment, and keep doing it while you work.

Blood loss is judged against the patient. A volume that would barely register in an adult may be a large share of a small child's circulating volume.

And the compensation point drives the most consequential decision you make. Children hold on, then crash. So transport decisions get made early, on mechanism and on the first impression, rather than after the child has deteriorated enough to make the decision obvious. If you are waiting for confirmation, you are waiting too long.

Finally, where your system provides one, transport to a facility with paediatric capability, and pre-alert.
read.standard: Trauma constitutes a leading cause of paediatric mortality, with blunt mechanisms predominating including falls, pedestrian injury, motor vehicle collision and cycling injury. Reduced body size distributes applied force across a greater proportion of the body, rendering multi-system injury the typical rather than exceptional presentation and requiring comprehensive assessment. The proportionally large, heavy head frequently leads in falls; head injury is common and often the most significant injury present, warranting careful monitoring of mental status. Skeletal and thoracic flexibility permits transmission of force to underlying organs without fracture, so absence of fracture does not exclude significant thoracic or abdominal visceral injury. Management proceeds on presumed mechanism, treating for potential injury rather than demonstrated injury, as paediatric patients conceal injury effectively before abrupt decompensation. Airway management follows paediatric principles: neutral positioning with shoulder padding and avoidance of over-extension. Hypothermia risk is elevated by exposure, clothing removal and surface area to mass ratio, and worsens haemorrhage and outcome; active covering and compartment warming are indicated throughout. Haemorrhage is assessed relative to patient size given small absolute circulating volume. Given the compensation pattern, transport decisions are made early on mechanism and initial impression rather than following demonstrated deterioration. Transport is directed to paediatric-capable facilities where the system provides them, with prearrival notification.

eli_new.analogy: An adult struck by a car may have one injured leg. A child struck by the same car has taken that force through everything at once.
eli_new.body: Assume the mechanism. Children conceal injury extremely well and then stop concealing it all at once, so treat what the forces could have done rather than what you can currently find.

story.dispatch: Engine 3 — child struck by a car at low speed, walking at the scene.
story.body:
The child was up and talking and somebody suggested waiting to see how things developed.

The officer asked what force had gone through that body and where it had gone.

They made the transport decision on the mechanism, which is the only time you get to make it early.
